coreTruths.title: Primary teeth are not just smaller permanent teeth: anatomy changes how disease behaves and how to cut a cavity
coreTruths.broaderContext: Primary teeth differ structurally from permanent ones in ways that change how disease progresses and how cavities should be designed. Adult-trained reflexes will overprep and expose the pulp.
coreTruths.body:
## Enamel is half the thickness, and the pulp is much closer

Enamel in primary teeth is roughly 1mm thick, half that of permanent teeth [1]. The pulp chamber is proportionately larger with more accentuated pulp horns [2]. That combination means caries reaches the pulp sooner and exposure during preparation is much more likely.

## Cut shallow and follow the contour, not a flat floor

Aim for only 0.5 to 1.0mm into dentine unless caries forces you deeper [2]. The pulpal outline follows the amelo-dentinal junction closely, so the cavity floor has to follow the external contour of the tooth in a wavy line, not a flat one, to avoid exposure [3].

## Broad flat contacts hide approximal caries

Contact points are broad and flat rather than tight, which makes interproximal caries hard to spot visually [4]. Bitewings are essential for diagnosis unless the dentition is spaced enough to see the surfaces directly [5].

## Younger alveolar bone is more permeable, so block injections are usually unnecessary

Alveolar bone is more permeable in younger children, so infiltration alone usually anaesthetises primary mandibular molars up to about 6 years of age [6]. The default reach for an inferior dental block is overkill at that age.

## Pulp death in primary molars shows up at the furcation, not the apex

The pulpal floor of primary molars is thin with accessory canals running into the furcation [7]. Pulp death in these teeth often shows up as inter-radicular radiolucency rather than apical, which matters when reading a radiograph in a young child.

citations.quote: (1) Enamel in 1° teeth is ~1mm thick, which is half that of 2° teeth.

(2) The pulp chamber in 1° teeth is proportionately larger, with more accentuated pulp horns. DE—three pulp horns MB, DB, and palatal. Lower DE—four pulp horns MB, ML, DB, and DL. These features mean that caries will affect the pulp sooner and there is a greater likelihood of pulp exposure during cavity preparation. Aim for only 0.5–1.0mm penetration into dentine, except where caries determines deeper preparation.
(3) This follows the amelo-dentinal junction more closely in 1° teeth, therefore cavity floor should follow external contour of tooth sinuously to avoid exposure.

(4) This makes detection of interproximal caries more difficult, and means that in 1° molars divergence of the buccal and lingual walls towards the approximal surface is necessary to ensure cavity margins are self-cleansing.
Bitewings are important for an accurate ∆ unless approximal surfaces of the 1° molars can be visualized (i.e. the dentition is spaced).
This is ↑ in younger children, thus it is usually possible to achieve local anaesthesia of 1° mandibular molars by infiltration alone, up to 6yrs of age.
(8) This may explain the greater incidence of inter-radicular involvement following pulp death.

coreTruths.title: Caries in primary molars can move from early dentine to pulp in under a year
coreTruths.broaderContext: Caries moves faster in primary teeth than adult-trained reflexes expect. That changes diagnosis, watch-and-wait thresholds, and what to do when a visit runs out of time.
coreTruths.body:
## Progress can outrun a six-month recall

Caries can progress from early dentine involvement to the pulp in less than a year in primary molars [1]. Thinner enamel, larger pulp horns, and a pulpal outline that hugs the ADJ all push the disease faster than in permanent teeth.

## Bitewings are not optional

Waiting for visible approximal caries is too late, the pulp is often already involved. Bitewings are essential for diagnosis unless the dentition is spaced enough to see the surfaces directly [2]. Marginal ridge breakdown in a primary molar is a high-probability sign of pulpal involvement [3], so it should trigger a pulp therapy or stainless steel crown discussion, not another plastic restoration.

## Sealing what you cannot finish today is buying time, not failing the visit

If cooperation runs out before the cavity is complete, the recommended move is to clear caries from the ADJ and place a GIC or zinc oxide dressing [4]. That is not a fallback, it produces a coronal seal that improves the chance of pulpal recovery and survival [5].

## Repair without prevention does not hold

Restorative care without prevention is of limited value because the disease keeps producing new lesions [6]. In many children with caries in primary molars, prevention alone is enough if oral hygiene is good [7]. Before signing up for a series of restorations, the first question is whether the disease has actually been controlled.

citations.quote: Rapid progression is especially common in 1° molars, with progress from early dentine involvement to pulpal involvement in <1yr in some cases.
Bitewings are important for an accurate ∆ unless approximal surfaces of the 1° molars can be visualized (i.e. the dentition is spaced).
In 1° molars destruction of the marginal ridge indicates a high probability of pulpal involvement.

If the child’s cooperation runs out before the cavity is completed, try and ensure all caries is removed from the ADJ and place a dressing of either zinc oxide or GIC. This should suffice for several visits, until you are ready to try again.
Produces a preliminary coronal seal, enhancing the chances of pulpal recovery and survival.
Restorative care (i.e. repair) without prevention is of limited value. Dental caries is treated by ‘preventive’ measures; ‘restoration’ primarily repairs the damage caused by the carious process.
In many circumstances, children with caries in 1° molars may be treated by prevention alone if oral hygiene is good.

coreTruths.title: Whether to extract or restore a primary tooth is multifactorial, not a default
coreTruths.broaderContext: Extract-versus-restore decisions in the primary dentition pull on age, medical history, cooperation, position in the arch, and the wider occlusion. There is no default answer.
coreTruths.body:
## The decision pulls on multiple factors at once

The call depends on age, medical history, parental motivation, extent and number of lesions, pain, position of the tooth in the arch, the permanent successor, and the wider malocclusion [1].

## Medical history can flip the decision both ways

In an immunocompromised patient or one at risk of endocarditis, primary pulp therapy is generally avoided in favour of extraction with appropriate precautions, because pulp therapy carries recurrent bacteraemia. The opposite call applies in haemophiliacs: keep primary teeth in until natural exfoliation rather than risk extraction bleeding [2].

## Position in the arch shapes the orthodontic consequences

Loss of primary incisors in early childhood has little orthodontic consequence, but extraction of C, D, or E in a crowded mouth localises the crowding [3]. The general teaching is to balance Cs (extract the contralateral) to prevent a centre-line shift [4], and to defer extraction of upper Es until the 6 has erupted [3], because the 6 will otherwise drift mesially.

## Cooperation outranks textbook symmetry

A happy and cooperative patient matters more in the long term than a perfectly balanced extraction pattern. Under local anaesthesia, leaving extractions unbalanced and monitoring for centre-line shift can be preferable to prolonging the chair time [5].

citations.quote: Despite a welcome reduction in the prevalence of dental decay, the dilemma of whether to restore or extract a 1° tooth is still all too familiar. In making a decision, a number of factors should be considered, including:

For patients where recurrent bacteraemia carries ↑ risks (e.g. immunocompromised, risk of endocarditis) it is generally considered that 1° tooth pulp therapy should be avoided, with extraction (taking appropriate precautions where necessary) often being more appropriate. Conversely, in haemophiliacs, extractions should be avoided and 1° teeth preserved, if possible, until their exfoliation. Prevention is particularly important in all such patients.

Although early loss of 1° incisors will have little effect, extraction of C, D, or E will, in a crowded case, lead to localization of the crowding. Extraction of Es, particularly in the upper arch, should be deferred, if possible, until the 6 has erupted.
In general, loss of Cs in a crowded patient should be balanced to prevent a centre-line shift.

So much for the theory; in practice, it should be remembered that a happy and cooperative patient is more important in the long term. When treating a child under local analgesia, leaving extractions unbalanced and monitoring for centre-line shift may be preferable to prolonging intervention in the dental chair.

coreTruths.title: Behaviour management is the prerequisite for treatment, not an extra
coreTruths.broaderContext: A child who will not cooperate cannot be treated, no matter the technical plan. Acclimatisation, language, and parental involvement are clinical tools, not soft skills.
coreTruths.body:
## Treat the patient, not the tooth

The principal aim is a healthy, functional dentition delivered to a happy and cooperative patient where possible, with prevention as priority [1]. Treatment plans are built visit by visit, starting simple and progressing at the child's pace [2].

## Reinforce the behaviour you want, ignore the rest

Praise good behaviour and ignore bad. Avoid rhetorical questions or offering choice where there is none [3]. If a child protests during treatment, abandoning the session and returning them to the parent inadvertently rewards the protest, so ensure something small is completed and praise that [4].

## Tell, show, do, and let the child have some control

Describe the procedure in language the child can understand, show the instrument, then do it [5]. Giving the child a stop signal, such as raising a hand, lowers anxiety because it puts them partly in charge [6].

## The first visit is for acclimatisation, not a full exam

For very young children a full dental examination is not essential if compliance is an issue. The emphasis is on acclimatisation, age-appropriate prevention, and rapport [7]. Children should first see a dentist by about 6 months of age, in line with the Dental Check by One initiative [7].

## GA is a last resort, with a real mortality risk

General anaesthesia should only be used when other methods are unsuitable. The risk of unexpected death of a healthy person under GA has been estimated at 3 to 4 in 1 million, and under sedation about 1 in 2 million [8]. Parents need that figure to make an informed decision.

citations.quote: Development and maintenance of healthy, functional, and aesthetic 1° and 2° dentitions. Freedom from pain and infection. A happy and cooperative patient, if possible. Prevention is priority.
Start with simple procedures (e.g. OHI) and progress, at child’s pace, to more complicated Rx.

Praise good behaviour (reinforcement …… Techniques for behaviour management, p. 60), ignore bad. Involve parents (they determine whether the child will return). Do not offer choice where there is none. Avoid rhetorical questions (‘Would you like to sit on my chair?’).

This is the strengthening of patterns of behaviour, usually by rewarding good behaviour with approval and praise. If a child protests and is uncooperative during Rx, do not immediately abandon the session and return them to the consolation of their parent, as this could inadvertently reinforce the undesirable behaviour. Try to ensure that something is completed (e.g. placing a dressing or even an examination) and focus on the successful completion of this, rather than the failure to complete what might have been originally planned.
Self-explanatory, but use language the child will understand.
Giving the child some control over the situation will also help them to relax, e.g. a stop signal such as raising their hand if they want you to stop for any reason (‘enhancing control’).

For infants and very young children a full dental examination is not essential if compliance is an issue. The emphasis should be on acclimatization, delivering age-appropriate preventive advice, and establishing rapport and a positive trusting professional relationship with the family.
Under GA has been estimated to be about 3 or 4 in 1 million. Under sedation has been estimated to be about 1 in 2 million.

coreTruths.title: Trauma to a primary tooth puts the permanent successor at risk
coreTruths.broaderContext: The primary tooth sits directly above a developing permanent successor. Treatment decisions after trauma are about protecting that successor first, the primary tooth second.
coreTruths.body:
## The successor outranks the primary tooth

In the primary dentition the aims after trauma are, in order: preserve the integrity of the permanent successor, then preserve the primary tooth if cooperation allows and it is compatible with the first aim [1]. When in doubt, extract the primary tooth [2].

## Intrusion is the most common primary tooth injury

Intrusion is the most common injury, accounting for over 60% [3]. If radiographs confirm the primary tooth has been forced into the follicle of the permanent successor, extract the primary incisor. Otherwise leave it and wait for spontaneous eruption between 1 and 6 months [3].

## Avulsed primary teeth are not replanted

Replantation of an avulsed primary tooth is not recommended because of the risk of damage to the permanent successor [4]. This is the opposite of the rule for permanent teeth and easy to confuse under pressure.

## Trauma in young children frequently scars the developing successor

In over half of children under 4 years, trauma to a primary tooth affects the underlying developing successor, with effects ranging from hypomineralisation and hypoplasia to dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development [5]. Parents need to be warned that what looks like a recovered baby tooth may show up later as a defect on the adult tooth.

citations.quote: 1° dentition: (i) preserve integrity of permanent successor; (ii) preserve 1° tooth if cooperation good and compatible with first aim.
There is a need to consider the effect of any proposed Rx upon the permanent successor. Splinting of 1° incisors is exceedingly difficult and not indicated. When in doubt, extract 1° tooth!

Most common injury (>60%). If X-ray confirms that tooth has been forced into follicle of 2° tooth, extract 1° incisor. Otherwise leave tooth and wait to see if spontaneous eruption will occur (between 1 and 6 months). Unfortunately, pulpal necrosis often follows, necessitating either pulp Rx (…… Pulp therapy for primary anterior teeth, p. 96) or extraction. Should the tooth fail to erupt, then extraction is indicated. It is prudent to warn parents about possible damage to underlying permanent tooth.
Replantation not recommended due to risk of damage to permanent successor.

In >50% of children <4yrs, trauma to a 1° tooth affects the underlying developing successor. The effect depends upon stage of development, type of injury and severity, Rx, and pulpal sequelae. Trauma can cause hypomineralization, hypoplasia (likelihood ↑ if <4yrs &/or injury more severe), dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development.

coreTruths.title: Avulsed permanent teeth: prognosis lives or dies on PDL viability in the first hour
coreTruths.broaderContext: Outcome after avulsion of a permanent tooth turns almost entirely on whether periodontal ligament cells survive. That makes the first 30 to 60 minutes the whole game.
coreTruths.body:
## Replant immediately, ideally at the scene

Avulsed permanent teeth should be replanted immediately [1]. PDL cells rarely survive more than 60 minutes extra-orally, so immediate replacement by whoever is at the scene is the treatment of choice [2].

## Storage medium is a hierarchy, not a tie

If replantation is not possible at the scene, prognosis runs saline > milk > water > air, with both tap water and dry storage rapidly damaging the periodontal cells [3].

## Splint flexibly and briefly

For a replanted tooth, flexible splinting for 7 to 10 days is the rule [4]. Prolonged or rigid splinting promotes ankylosis, which is exactly the failure mode you are trying to avoid [4].

## Pulp behaviour depends on apex maturity

In a tooth with a closed apex, or any tooth with an extra-alveolar period beyond 30 minutes, treat as non-vital and extirpate the pulp within 7 to 10 days [5]. In an open apex replanted within 30 minutes, revascularisation is possible, so wait and watch.

## Long-term survival follows root maturity

If the protocol is followed, medium-term survival is reasonable but long-term survival is generally poor [6]. Five-year survival is around 60% with incomplete root formation and 80% with complete root formation [7]. Even when the long-term outlook is bad, replantation is still preferable because failure by replacement resorption is slow and preserves alveolar bulk for future prosthetic replacement [8].

citations.quote: Avulsed permanent teeth should be replanted immediately.
Time from loss to reimplantation—as PDL cells rarely survive >60min extra-orally, immediate replacement (by whoever is available at the scene) is the Rx of choice.
Storage medium—prognosis saline > milk > water > air (both tap-water and dry storage rapidly damage periodontal cells).
Splinting time—7–10 days flexible splinting. Prolonged splinting may promote ankylosis.

If apex closed (or tooth with open apex, but extra-alveolar period >30min) extirpate pulp within 7–10 days, clean canal. If an intermediate dressing is required or monitoring inflammatory resorption, place an initial intra-canal dressing of calcium hydroxide. A mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) plug is the gold standard now. GDPs should always dress a tooth before referring to an appropriate provider to place MTA.
If the described procedure is followed, medium-term survival is relatively good but long-term survival is generally poor.
Incomplete root formation: 60% survive 5yrs. Complete root formation: 80% survive 5yrs.

Long-term survival is closely related to extra-alveolar dry-storage time. Teeth stored dry for >30min have a very poor long-term prognosis, but replantation is always preferable, as failure is usually by replacement resorption which is slow (i.e. tooth may last several years) and maintains bulk of alveolus (facilitates future prosthetic replacement).

coreTruths.title: Severe early childhood caries is a feeding-pattern disease, not just a brushing problem
coreTruths.broaderContext: Severe early childhood caries is driven by frequent sugar exposure and overnight feeding, not by lazy brushing. The fix is in the bottle and the bedtime routine, not the toothbrush.
coreTruths.body:
## Aetiology is frequency of sugar plus reduced salivary flow

The core driver is frequent ingestion of sugar with or without reduced salivary flow [1]. Saliva flow drops during sleep, which is why overnight feeding is so destructive.

## The classic bottle-mouth pattern is not random

Nursing-bottle caries describes the pattern that follows frequent consumption of a sugar-containing drink, especially from a feeding bottle, often with the child falling asleep with the bottle and suckling overnight [2]. The maxillary primary incisors go first, then the first primary molars in more severe cases. The mandibular incisors are relatively protected by the tongue and saliva [2].

## Prolonged on-demand breastfeeding can also drive ECC

Early childhood caries can also be associated with prolonged breastfeeding beyond age 2 years, particularly in children over 1 year who suckle frequently overnight [3]. Breastfeeding is still optimal and should be encouraged, so the conversation has to be handled with sensitivity rather than blame [3].

## Sugar-based medicines are a hidden contributor

Severe ECC may also be associated with prolonged and frequent intake of sugar-based medications [3]. Long-term liquid medication is now a known cariogenic risk, and sugar-free preparations should be prescribed where possible [4]. Rinsing or brushing after a sugar-based medicine does not significantly reduce caries [4], so the answer is changing the medicine, not the brushing.

citations.quote: Frequent ingestion of sugar &/or reduced salivary flow.

Terms used to describe patterns of early childhood caries (ECC) associated with frequent consumption of a sugar-containing drink, especially from a feeding-bottle. Commonly the child falls asleep with the bottle of juice or milk and suckles during the night. Possibly related to the relatively high levels of lactose in breast milk. The WHO recommends mothers exclusively breastfeed their child for the first 6 months before introducing nutritious complementary foods. Characteristically, starts with the maxillary 1° incisors, but in more severe cases the first 1° molars are also involved. The mandibular incisors are relatively protected by the tongue and saliva.

Severe ECC may also be associated with the prolonged and frequent intake of sugar-based medications; however, both pharmaceutical companies and doctors are more aware of the problem and the number of alternative sugar-free preparations is i. See Table 3.6 for a list (p. 119). Recent studies have confirmed that ECC may be associated with prolonged breastfeeding beyond age 2yrs. Children >1yr old who suckle frequently during the night may be most at risk. Breastfeeding is considered to be optimal for babies and should be encouraged. Counselling about the possible role of on-demand breastfeeding in ECC should be approached with sensitivity and understanding.

The potential cariogenic effect of long-term medication sweetened with sugar is now well recognized. Therefore sugar-free preparations should be prescribed whenever possible. Unfortunately, there is no evidence that rinsing out or brushing the teeth after use of a sugar-based medicine will significantly ↓ the incidence of caries.

coreTruths.title: Developmental enamel and dentine defects need early recognition because protection changes long-term outcome
coreTruths.broaderContext: MIH, amelogenesis imperfecta, and dentinogenesis imperfecta share a common clinical lesson: weak hard tissue wears fast, so early protection prevents irreversible loss.
coreTruths.body:
## MIH is common and 6s break down post-eruptively

Molar incisor hypomineralisation primarily affects the first permanent molars, with about half of affected children also showing defects on permanent incisors [1]. Prevalence has been reported at 14.2% [2]. Affected 6s carry hypomineralised enamel that ranges from discoloration to severe dysplasia with post-eruptive breakdown, with increased sensitivity and increased secondary caries [1]. Treatment options include intracoronal restoration, stainless steel crowns, microabrasion, vital bleaching, resin infiltrate, or extraction, depending on aesthetics and prognosis [3].

## Amelogenesis imperfecta affects both dentitions

Amelogenesis imperfecta usually affects both primary and permanent dentitions and all the teeth [4]. The clinical picture varies hugely between the hypoplastic, hypocalcified, and hypomaturation subtypes, so specialist advice is wise for all but the mildest forms [4]. In severe cases, stainless steel crowns and composite resin are used to maintain molars and permanent incisors until the child is older and definitive restorations become possible [4].

## Dentinogenesis imperfecta wears fast because the ADJ fails

Dentinogenesis imperfecta affects both dentitions, with opalescent brown or blue crowns, bulbous crown form, short roots, and narrow flame-shaped pulps. The amelo-dentinal junction is abnormal, so the enamel flakes off, leading to rapid wear of the soft dentine [5].

## Early recognition is the lever

Early recognition and treatment of amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta are important to prevent rapid tooth wear [6]. Prevention is a priority in any child with developmental anomalies to minimise secondary caries, tooth surface loss, and periodontal disease [7]. Multidisciplinary management coordinating paediatric, restorative, and orthodontic input is the norm rather than the exception [7].

citations.quote: Primarily affects 6s, but ~50% also have defects on permanent incisors. Affected 6s have hypomineralized defects of enamel, varying from discoloration to severe enamel dysplasia with post-eruptive breakdown. Sensitivity i, 2° caries i. Defects may affect anything from one to all 6s.
Aetiology unknown. Prevalence ↑ over the past two decades in developed countries. Prevalence 14.2%.

Rx options include intracoronal restoration, SS crowns, microabrasion, vital bleaching, resin infiltrate, or extraction, depending on aesthetics and prognosis (…… Extraction of poor-quality first permanent molars, p. 140). Partial composite veneers can be considered to repair post-eruptive breakdown of incisors.

Usually both 1° and 2° dentitions and all the teeth are affected. The different subgroups give rise to a wide variation in clinical presentation, ranging from discoloration to soft &/or deficient enamel. It is therefore difficult to make general recommendations, but it is wise to seek specialist advice for all but the mildest forms. Rx: in more severe cases, SS crowns and composite resin can be used to maintain molars and 2° inc, prior to more permanent restorations when child is older.

Affected teeth have an opalescent brown or blue hue, bulbous crowns, short roots, and narrow flame-shaped pulps. The ADJ is abnormal, which results in the enamel flaking off, leading to rapid wear of the soft dentine. Rx: along similar lines as for severe amelogenesis.
Early recognition and Rx of amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta is important to prevent rapid tooth wear.
Prevention is a priority in children with developmental dental anomalies to minimize the risk of 2° caries, tooth surface loss, and periodontal disease.
